name: Valid Accounts
overview: Adversaries obtain and reuse legitimate credentials to gain access, and the technique spans four MITRE tactics at once — Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Stealth — because a valid login doesn't just get an attacker in, it also lets them stay, escalate, and blend into normal activity all with the same mechanism. This is the technique family everything T1003 and T1558 feed into: those packs are about obtaining credentials, this one is about what happens once an attacker actually uses them. The four sub-techniques below split by account tier — default, domain, local, and cloud — because each has a different blast radius and a different detection surface when compromised.

prerequisite_concepts.term: Why this is the highest-success-rate technique in the framework
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: No exploit, no malware, no vulnerability required — just a username and password (or a token) that happens to be real. Industry testing has repeatedly found Valid Accounts succeeding in the overwhelming majority of tested environments, and a large share of real intrusions rely on legitimate credentials rather than malware or exploits at all. That's the throughline for this whole pack: it's not that defenses fail to stop an attack, it's that from the system's point of view there's no attack to stop — just a login.

prerequisite_concepts.term: The four account tiers and why blast radius differs
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: A default account (factory-preset, often never rotated) is usually scoped to one device or appliance. A local account is scoped to one machine, but password reuse across many machines turns it into something much bigger. A domain account is scoped to the whole Active Directory domain by design. A cloud account can be scoped to an entire tenant, and if federated with on-premises AD, can bridge both worlds at once. The sub-technique split below exists because the right response to a compromise scales completely differently depending on which tier is involved.

A stolen credential produces logon events that are byte-for-byte identical to a legitimate one — same protocol, same success code, same absence of any exploit artifact. There is no malware signature to catch and no anomalous process to flag. This is why every detection strategy across this pack is behavioral rather than signature-based: unusual timing, impossible geographic travel between two sign-ins, a service account suddenly used interactively, an account authenticating to far more hosts than its normal pattern. The whole discipline shifts from "is this bad" to "is this normal for this specific identity."

prerequisite_concepts.term: MFA as the actual circuit-breaker, and why it isn't always one
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: Nearly every mitigation across all four sub-techniques below leads back to multi-factor authentication, because a password alone stops being sufficient the moment a second factor is required — which is exactly why credential-only theft (T1003, password spraying, phishing) increasingly isn't enough on its own anymore. But MFA isn't absolute: session/refresh tokens issued after a successful MFA challenge can themselves be stolen and reused for their remaining lifetime without ever re-proving the second factor, and MFA fatigue attacks (bombarding a user with push notifications until they approve one) target the human in the loop rather than the cryptography. Both are why user training on push-notification hygiene shows up as a named mitigation here, not just technical controls.

subtechniques.name: Default Accounts
subtechniques.overview: Every system ships with at least one factory-preset account — Guest or Administrator on Windows, root on Linux/ESXi/AWS, a default service account in Kubernetes — and the risk exists from the moment the system is deployed, before an attacker does anything at all. Some default accounts aren't even part of the original install: ESXi automatically creates a vpxuser account the moment a host is connected to vCenter, a side effect of integration rather than initial setup, which makes it exactly the kind of account an inventory audit is likely to miss.

concepts.term: A vulnerability that predates the attacker
concepts.explanation: Unlike almost every other technique in this guide, the exposure here isn't created by anything the victim organization did wrong during the intrusion — it's a decision (or a missed step) from before the attacker ever showed up: a vendor shipping a predictable default credential, and nobody rotating it before production. That timing matters operationally: finding and closing this gap is a proactive inventory exercise, not something that only becomes visible during incident response.

concepts.term: Integration-created accounts are the easy-to-miss variant
concepts.explanation: vpxuser is the clean example: it doesn't exist until an ESXi host is connected to vCenter, at which point it's created automatically with vCenter-scoped privileges. Because it wasn't part of the initial OS install, it's exactly the kind of account a first-pass "list default accounts" audit misses — the audit has to account for what gets created by every downstream integration, not just what ships in the box.

concepts.term: Kubernetes' own default service account is a default-account risk hiding in plain sight
concepts.explanation: Every namespace gets a `default` ServiceAccount automatically, and unless a pod spec explicitly sets `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, Kubernetes mounts that account's API token into the container's filesystem whether the workload needs cluster-API access or not. A compromised pod running with no legitimate reason to talk to the Kubernetes API can still read that token straight off disk and start making authenticated calls against the cluster — the exact same 'default credential nobody rotated or scoped down' pattern as a factory admin password, just expressed as a Kubernetes primitive instead of a device login.

procedure_examples.activity: Exploited default usernames and passwords in externally-exposed IP cameras for initial access.
Leveraged default credentials on myWebMethods and QLogic web management interfaces.
Activated the built-in DefaultAccount via PowerShell to access targeted Exchange servers over RDP.
Infected WinCC machines by exploiting a hardcoded database server password.
Harvested and abused vCenter Server service accounts, including vpxuser.

data_sources.detail: Interactive or remote logon by Guest or built-in Administrator outside any documented maintenance window.
Password-based (not key-based) logins for the root account specifically, which most hardened Linux hosts should never see.
root or vpxuser logins, especially from a source inconsistent with the vCenter server itself.
Authentication using known default credential pairs (admin/admin, cisco/cisco-style patterns) on routers, firewalls, and switches.

detection_queries.title: Interactive Logon by Built-in Administrator or Guest
detection_queries.description: Flags interactive or remote-interactive logons using the built-in Administrator or Guest account, both of which should be disabled or never used directly in a well-managed environment.
detection_queries.query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4624
| where LogonType in (2, 10)
| where TargetUserName in~ ("Administrator", "Guest", "DefaultAccount")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, TargetUserName, LogonType, IpAddress
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection_queries.title: SSH Password Login as root
detection_queries.description: Flags password-authenticated root SSH logins, which should be rare-to-nonexistent on a hardened host that relies on key-based auth.
detection_queries.query:
title: SSH Password Login as root
id: 3f8a6c2e-9b4d-4e1a-8c7f-2d6b9a4e3c50
status: stable
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  product: linux
  service: auth
detection:
  selection:
    - 'Accepted password for root'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Break-glass emergency access on hosts that don't yet have key-based auth fully enforced
level: high
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1078.001

false_positives: Documented maintenance-window use of a default account by IT staff, particularly during initial provisioning before individual accounts are set up
vCenter's own vpxuser performing normal SSO/management operations against ESXi hosts it legitimately manages
response_steps: Disable or rotate the default account's credentials immediately — don't just monitor it, since there's rarely a legitimate reason for continued default-account use
Review exactly what the account accessed during the suspected compromise window
Audit the environment for other default accounts that have never been touched since install, on this system and elsewhere
For integration-created accounts (vpxuser-style), verify the parent integration itself (vCenter, in that example) wasn't the actual point of compromise

mitigations.name: Multi-factor Authentication
mitigations.detail: Apply MFA to default accounts so a compromised default credential alone isn't sufficient.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Change default username/password combinations immediately after installation, before production deployment.

related.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
related.relation: A common immediate next step once default local credentials are confirmed valid — connecting to admin shares with them.

hypothesis.statement: Guest, the built-in Administrator, DefaultAccount, or a device's factory root account authenticates interactively or remotely outside a documented provisioning or maintenance window.
hypothesis.rationale: Because none of these accounts should be in routine use once an environment is properly configured, this hunt is best run as an ongoing detection rather than a one-time sweep -- recurring hits point to a provisioning gap worth fixing at the source.

subtechniques.name: Domain Accounts
subtechniques.overview: Domain accounts — user, administrator, and service accounts managed through Active Directory — are compromised primarily via OS credential dumping or password reuse, and once obtained they work across every domain-joined host that trusts the same directory. That single-compromise-many-doors property is exactly why domain account abuse is the connective tissue between an initial foothold and full lateral movement across an environment.

concepts.explanation: A local account's usefulness ends at the machine it's defined on. A domain account authenticates against the same Active Directory trust from any domain-joined host, which means one set of stolen domain credentials can potentially reach every system in the environment, not just the one it was harvested from — the entire reason domain credential theft (T1003.001, T1003.003, T1003.006) is worth the effort in the first place.

concepts.term: Domain service accounts as the quiet, high-privilege blind spot
concepts.explanation: Service accounts aren't meant for interactive human logon, so they typically never face an MFA challenge, get created once and forgotten, and are frequently over-privileged because nobody wants to be the one who breaks a production service by trimming its rights. That combination — high privilege, no MFA, rarely audited — is exactly why Kerberoasting (T1558.003) specifically targets these accounts: they're the domain-account subset most likely to have a weak password and the most to gain from cracking it.

procedure_examples.activity: Used administrative accounts including Domain Admin for lateral movement.
Used domain administrator accounts after dumping LSASS memory.
Accessed administrative domain accounts using stolen credentials.
Used a domain administrator account to facilitate lateral network movement.
Authenticated to compromised network devices using domain accounts.

data_sources.detail: The same domain account authenticating to an unusually large number of distinct hosts in a short window — the core lateral-movement signature.
Off-hours logons, or two logons for the same account from geographically implausible locations within a short window.
Domain account logons on Linux hosts joined to AD, outside that account's typical access pattern.

detection_queries.title: Domain Account Authenticating to Many Distinct Hosts
detection_queries.description: Flags a single account logging onto an unusually high number of distinct hosts in a short window — the lateral-movement-via-valid-account signature.
detection_queries.query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4624
| where LogonType in (3, 10)
| summarize DistinctHosts = dcount(Computer), Hosts = make_set(Computer) by TargetUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| where DistinctHosts >= 6
| order by DistinctHosts desc

detection_queries.title: Domain Account Lateral Movement Fan-Out
detection_queries.description: Vendor-agnostic version of the many-hosts-one-account pattern.
detection_queries.query:
title: Domain Account Authenticating to Many Distinct Hosts
id: 6b3e9c4a-8f2d-4c7e-9a1b-5d3f8c6e2a90
status: experimental
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4624
    LogonType:
      - 3
      - 10
  condition: selection | count(Computer) by TargetUserName > 5
falsepositives:
  - IT staff performing legitimate multi-host maintenance in a short window
  - A domain service account running a scheduled task across many hosts (patch management, monitoring agents)
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.lateral_movement
  - attack.t1078.002

false_positives: IT staff performing legitimate multi-host maintenance or deployment work in a short window
A domain service account running a scheduled task (patch management, monitoring, backup agents) across many hosts as its normal function
response_steps: Map every host the account authenticated to during the suspected window — that's the actual scope of the incident, not just the original foothold
Reset the account's password and, if it's a privileged account, treat this as a potential domain-wide exposure
Check for follow-on DCSync or Golden/Silver Ticket activity if the account had domain admin rights
Review whether an MFA gap (legacy protocol, exempted account) is what allowed the credential to be used without a second factor

mitigations.name: Multi-factor Authentication
mitigations.detail: Reduces the risk of a stolen domain credential being sufficient on its own.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Enforce complex, unique, regularly rotated passwords.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Audit permission levels; avoid placing user/admin accounts in local administrator groups across systems.

mitigations.name: User Account Management
mitigations.detail: Regularly review domain accounts; remove or disable inactive ones.

related.name: DCSync
related.relation: The usual escalation once a domain admin account is already compromised — pulling every other credential in the domain.

related.name: Kerberoasting
related.relation: The primary path to compromising a domain service account specifically, rather than a human one.

hypothesis.statement: A single domain account successfully authenticates to more than five distinct hosts within a thirty-minute window, outside the behavior of known IT deployment tooling or monitoring agents.
hypothesis.rationale: Baseline this threshold against your own environment before trusting it at face value -- patch-management and EDR service accounts routinely produce exactly this fan-out pattern, so the exclusion list matters more than the threshold itself.

subtechniques.name: Local Accounts
subtechniques.overview: Local accounts are configured per machine for standard users, remote support, services, and administration. They're scoped to a single system by design, but two things turn that narrow scope into something much bigger: password reuse across machines (one host's local hash unlocks every host that shares the same password), and dormant accounts belonging to people who've left the organization but whose accounts were never disabled.

concepts.term: Password reuse is what actually breaks the scoping
concepts.explanation: A local account is only supposed to work on the machine it's defined on. Before centralized local-admin-password management (LAPS) became standard practice, it was extremely common for IT to set the exact same local administrator password across an entire fleet during imaging — meaning one host's SAM dump (T1003.002) doesn't just compromise that host, it compromises every host sharing that password, which is functionally identical to a domain-wide credential despite never touching Active Directory at all.

concepts.term: Dormant accounts as a stealth channel
concepts.explanation: APT29 has specifically targeted accounts belonging to former employees whose accounts remain enabled on the system — nobody is watching for logons on an identity that isn't supposed to exist anymore, which is exactly the point. A dormant account isn't a technical vulnerability; it's a monitoring blind spot created by an incomplete offboarding process, and it's one of the few sub-techniques in this pack where the fix (disable unused accounts) is entirely process, not technology.

procedure_examples.activity: Targets dormant or inactive user accounts belonging to individuals no longer at the organization for access and persistence.
Deployed the GREASE tool to add Windows admin accounts specifically to enable RDP persistence.
Used valid local credentials with PsExec and wmic to propagate across systems as a worm.
Exploited compromised credentials to operate as SYSTEM on Exchange servers.
Exploited local accounts sharing identical passwords across victim networks.

data_sources.detail: A local account authenticating from a source or at a time inconsistent with normal use for that specific account.

One local account name successfully authenticating across many distinct hosts in a short window — the local-password-reuse signature, functionally identical in shape to the domain-account lateral-movement pattern but involving no domain account at all.
Absence of LAPS-managed rotation on a host is itself a risk indicator worth tracking, not just a data source for detecting abuse after the fact.

detection_queries.title: Local Account Authenticating Across Many Distinct Hosts
detection_queries.description: Flags a local (non-domain) account name succeeding at authentication on an unusually high number of distinct hosts — the password-reuse-without-LAPS signature.
detection_queries.query:
title: Local Account Password Reuse Across Hosts
id: 8c4d9b2e-6f3a-4e7c-9d1b-3f6a8c2e9d40
status: experimental
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4624
    LogonType:
      - 3
      - 10
  filter_domain:
    TargetDomainName: 'CORP'
  condition: selection and not filter_domain | count(Computer) by TargetUserName > 5
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate remote-support tooling that authenticates with a standard local support account by design, across many hosts
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1078.003

false_positives: Legitimate remote-support or helpdesk tooling that authenticates with a standard local support account across many hosts by design
Break-glass local admin usage during an outage when domain authentication is unavailable
response_steps: Determine whether local admin password reuse is the actual root cause — if so, the incident scope is every host sharing that password, not just the one first seen
Deploy or verify LAPS (or equivalent) is actually enforced across the fleet, not just configured
Disable dormant accounts belonging to former employees or decommissioned service integrations
Rotate the specific compromised local account everywhere it's reused, not just on the originally affected host

mitigations.name: Multi-factor Authentication
mitigations.detail: Deploy MFA on local accounts via mobile authenticators or hardware tokens where supported.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Mandate complex, unique passwords for local administrator accounts across all networked systems.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Implement LAPS to prevent local admin credential reuse across the domain; audit local account permissions regularly.

mitigations.name: User Account Management
mitigations.detail: Remove inactive or unused accounts to reduce the attack surface.

related.name: Security Account Manager
related.relation: The usual source of the local hash whose reuse across hosts this sub-technique depends on.

related.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
related.relation: The common next step once local admin credential reuse across a fleet is confirmed.

hypothesis.statement: The same local account name authenticates successfully across more than five distinct hosts within a short window, and LAPS or an equivalent local-admin-rotation control is not confirmed deployed on those hosts.
hypothesis.rationale: If this hunt returns a real hit, the finding usually isn't 'this one host is compromised' -- it's 'local admin password reuse exists across this entire fleet,' which changes the remediation scope from one machine to every machine sharing that password.

subtechniques.name: Cloud Accounts
subtechniques.overview: Cloud accounts exist purely in a cloud provider or SaaS application, or as a hybrid identity federated/synced with on-premises Active Directory. Compromise happens through brute force, phishing, leaked keys, or token theft, and once an attacker holds one, they can create long-lasting credentials, bypass MFA by stealing an already-authenticated session token, assume elevated permissions through misconfigured roles, and — if the account is federated — pivot between cloud and on-premises infrastructure using the same identity.

concepts.term: Federation makes this a bridge, not just a cloud-side problem
concepts.explanation: Azure AD Connect / Entra Connect continuously syncs identities between on-premises Active Directory and a cloud tenant. A compromised synced account — or worse, the sync service account itself — can be used to pivot in both directions, which is exactly why Storm-0501 specifically targeted Entra Connect access rather than treating it as just another cloud account: it's the one identity that legitimately crosses the boundary security teams usually treat as two separate trust zones.

concepts.term: Token theft is the cloud-native equivalent of Pass-the-Ticket
concepts.explanation: Modern cloud authentication issues a long-lived session or refresh token once MFA succeeds, so the app doesn't re-prompt for every action. Stealing that token — from a compromised device, a malicious OAuth app grant, or an adversary-in-the-middle phishing kit — lets an attacker act as the user for the token's remaining lifetime without ever facing the MFA challenge again. It's functionally identical to stealing a Kerberos ticket instead of a password: the proof-of-authentication itself, not the credential that produced it, becomes the thing worth stealing.

concepts.term: Legacy authentication protocols: the MFA bypass hiding in plain sight
concepts.explanation: Modern cloud sign-in enforces MFA at the identity provider itself — the login flow routes through it, and it's the one that issues the challenge. Legacy protocols (POP3, IMAP, SMTP AUTH, older Exchange ActiveSync/MAPI, and Basic Authentication generally) were built before that model existed: they authenticate with a bare username and password sent directly to the mail/app server, bypassing the identity provider's login flow entirely. The practical result is that an account can have MFA fully configured and still be completely accessible with just a stolen password, through a protocol that was never capable of asking for a second factor in the first place — which is exactly why disabling legacy auth outright is treated as more effective than any amount of MFA enforcement layered on top of it.

concepts.term: Service principals: the non-human blind spot, cloud edition
concepts.explanation: Service principals and managed identities are the cloud analogue of domain service accounts — they hold powerful API permissions, can't respond to an MFA prompt because there's no human behind them, and are easy to create without drawing attention. APT29 didn't need to steal an existing one during the SolarWinds compromise; using a compromised O365 admin account, they simply created a new Service Principal with the access they wanted, which is a persistence mechanism as much as an access one.

concepts.term: The Primary Refresh Token is a distinct, more powerful artifact than a browser session cookie
concepts.explanation: On a Windows device that's Azure AD joined or hybrid joined, Microsoft's own token broker issues a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) — a device-bound JWT, backed by a TPM-protected session key, that underpins single sign-on across every Microsoft app on that device and stands in for both the user's and the device's identity at once. Tools like ROADtoken and AADInternals can extract the PRT and its session key directly from a compromised device (via Cobalt Strike or similar tooling) and mint fresh SSO tokens from it — a materially more powerful theft than lifting a single browser session cookie, since a PRT effectively satisfies the device-compliance/hybrid-join condition many Conditional Access policies specifically require, without ever putting hands on the TPM-sealed key itself.

procedure_examples.activity: Leveraged compromised Microsoft Entra ID accounts to pivot within victim environments.
Leveraged compromised accounts to access Microsoft Entra Connect and abused Global Administrator accounts lacking MFA.
Used a compromised O365 administrator account to create a new Service Principal.
Utilized valid cloud accounts for initial access, including AWS credentials obtained from public repositories.
Employed compromised credentials to access cloud assets within target organizations.

data_sources.detail: Impossible-travel sign-ins (two locations too far apart for the time between them) and legacy authentication protocol usage that bypasses modern MFA enforcement.
New Service Principal / app registration creation, especially by an account not normally responsible for that action.
API calls or IAM policy changes outside an identity's normal scope of activity, including from a service account suddenly performing interactive-style actions.

detection_queries.title: Impossible Travel Between Two Sign-Ins for the Same Account
detection_queries.description: Flags two successful sign-ins for the same account from geographically implausible locations given the time between them.
detection_queries.query:
SigninLogs
| where ResultType == 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location=tostring(LocationDetails.city)
| sort by UserPrincipalName, TimeGenerated asc
| serialize
| extend PrevTime = prev(TimeGenerated), PrevLocation = prev(Location), PrevUser = prev(UserPrincipalName)
| where UserPrincipalName == PrevUser and Location != PrevLocation
| extend GapMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, PrevTime)
| where GapMinutes < 60
| project UserPrincipalName, TimeGenerated, Location, PrevLocation, GapMinutes

detection_queries.title: New Service Principal Created by Non-Standard Actor
detection_queries.description: Flags Azure AD service principal / app registration creation, a common cloud persistence pattern.
detection_queries.query:
title: New Azure AD Service Principal Created
id: 4e9c7a3d-6b8f-4c2e-9a1d-7f3b6c9e4a20
status: experimental
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  category: application
  product: azure
  service: azuread
detection:
  selection:
    OperationName: 'Add service principal'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate application onboarding and DevOps automation creating service principals as part of normal deployment pipelines
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1078.004

false_positives: Legitimate VPN or corporate proxy exit-node changes producing apparent (but false) geo-travel anomalies
Application onboarding and DevOps automation legitimately creating new service principals as part of a deployment pipeline
Break-glass emergency access accounts intentionally exempted from conditional access/MFA policies
response_steps: Revoke active sessions and tokens for the account immediately — a password reset alone does not invalidate an already-issued session token
Review IAM/role and conditional-access policy changes made during the suspected compromise window
If the account is federated, check Entra Connect/AD Connect configuration for tampering and treat this as a potential bridge into on-premises infrastructure too
Audit for newly created service principals, app registrations, or long-lived access keys created during the window

mitigations.name: Account Use Policies
mitigations.detail: Implement conditional access policies blocking logins from non-compliant devices or outside defined IP ranges.

mitigations.name: Active Directory Configuration
mitigations.detail: Disable legacy authentication protocols that lack MFA support.

mitigations.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
mitigations.detail: Enforce MFA for cloud accounts, especially privileged ones, with auditing.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Routinely review privileged role assignments; implement just-in-time temporary access rather than permanent role grants.

related.name: Cached Domain Credentials
related.relation: In hybrid-identity environments, on-prem credential theft and cloud account compromise are two views of the same federated identity.

related.name: Cloud API
related.relation: The execution surface these stolen cloud credentials are actually used against once obtained.

hypothesis.statement: The same identity successfully authenticates from two locations whose distance makes the observed travel time physically implausible.
hypothesis.rationale: Exclude known corporate VPN egress and CDN/proxy ranges before treating a hit as a compromise -- those are, in practice, the majority of false positives against this specific hypothesis in most tenants.
